extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating objective/secondary considerations (unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, etc.) in determining nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 during patent examination and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater than expected results are evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: “A greater than expected result are evidence of nonobviousness” — evidence that results exceed what would have been expected from the prior art (including synergism) can be persuasive of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must show results were greater than expected from the prior art to an unobvious extent and provide a significant, practical advantage. A greater-than-additive effect may be expected or unexpected; applicants must demonstrate unexpectedness. (Cites: In re Corkill; Merck v. Biocraft; Ex parte NutraSweet.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of a property shared with the prior art is evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexpected superiority in a property the claimed compound shares with prior art can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness (no set number of examples required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative data showing improved effectiveness over the closest prior art may suffice even if performance on other properties is average. (Cites: In re Chupp; Ex parte A.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of an unexpected property is evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed invention possesses a property not possessed by the prior art, that presence of an unexpected property supports nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected presence need not automatically establish nonobviousness; context and weight of other evidence matter. (Cites: In re Papesch; Ex parte Thumm; In re Payne.) See MPEP §2145 for latent properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of an expected property is evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed invention lacks a property that would have been expected from the prior art, that absence may be evidence of unobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that prior art would have led to an expectation that the claimed compound had the property; show it does not. (Cites: Ex parte Mead Johnson & Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on applicant to establish results are unexpected and significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant must establish that differences in results are unexpected and of both statistical and practical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere conclusions in briefs/specifications are insufficient; declarations and data must establish unexpectedness and practical significance. (Cites: Ex parte Gelles; Ex parte C; In re Nolan; In re Eli Lilly.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants have burden of explaining proffered data
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellants/applicants bear the burden of explaining data in any declaration offered as evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations must be accompanied by explanation of the data's meaning and relevance. (Cites: Ex parte Ishizaka.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing expected and unexpected properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected and expected properties must be weighed together against the prima facie case of obviousness in the final determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected properties must have significance equal to or greater than expected properties to rebut obviousness. Examples where unexpected properties were outweighed by expected advantages are given. (Cites: In re May; In re Nolan; In re Eli Lilly.) See MPEP §716.01(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct and indirect comparative tests are probative of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct or indirect comparisons of the claimed invention with the closest prior art, commensurate in scope with the claims, are valid probative evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative testing (direct or indirect) can rebut prima facie obviousness; must be commensurate in scope. (Cites: In re Boesch; In re Blondel; In re Fouche.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of an intermediate may be shown by end-product unexpected properties when nexus is established
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexpected properties of an end product may establish patentability of an intermediate if one of ordinary skill would ascribe the intermediate as the contributing cause and a nexus is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must identify the cause of the unexpected activity/property and establish a nexus between intermediate and end product. (Cites: In re Magerlein.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected beneficial results are evidence of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Beneficial results that would have been expected from the prior art are evidence supporting obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed beneficial effect is taught or would have been expected, it weighs toward obviousness. (Cites: In re Gershon; Ex parte Blanc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results must be commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness (including unexpected results) must be commensurate in scope with the claims they are offered to support (i.e., occur over the claimed range).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing unexpected results for only a narrow or different scope than claimed may be insufficient to rebut an obviousness rejection. Provide testing across the claimed range or explain why narrower data are predictive. (Cites: In re Clemens; In re Peterson; In re Grasselli.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness of a genus or broad range may sometimes be supported by species or narrower-range data
rubrics_metrics.description: Data showing unexpected results for a species or narrower range can support nonobviousness of a genus or broader range if one of ordinary skill could determine a trend allowing reasonable extension of probative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited exemplification must show a trend that would allow extension; insufficient exemplification across the genus invalidates reliance. (Cites: In re Kollman; In re Lindner.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating criticality of a claimed range
rubrics_metrics.description: To show criticality of a claimed range, applicants should compare sufficient tests inside and outside the claimed range to demonstrate the criticality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviations from examples, lack of trend, or insufficient comparative testing should be noted and explained; otherwise rejections may be affirmed. (Cites: In re Hill; Finley; In re Armstrong.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed invention may be compared with prior art closer than that applied by the examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may compare their invention with prior art that is more closely related to the invention than the reference used by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons with closer art can be persuasive in rebutting the examiner's prima facie case. (Cites: In re Holladay; Ex parte Humber.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparisons when there are two equally close prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing unexpected results over one of two equally close prior art references will not rebut a prima facie case unless the teachings of the two references are sufficiently similar that testing one would inform about the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If testing less than all cited compounds, the testing must permit a conclusion about relative effectiveness across the closest prior art. (Cites: In re Johnson; In re Payne.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed invention need only be compared with existing prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are not required to compare the claimed invention with subject matter that does not exist in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison should be to the closest existing prior art; the PTO cannot require comparison to hypothetical inventions. (Cites: In re Geiger; In re Chapman.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages disclosed or inherent in the record must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence/arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded; the totality of the record is considered in obviousness determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undisclosed advantages or inherent properties may be relevant and should be considered; specification need not disclose proportions or critical values to permit applicant to present evidence of criticality. (Cites: In re Chu; In re Zenitz; Ex parte Sasajima; In re Saunders.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration or affidavit form required for probative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence submitted to rebut obviousness should be in declaration or affidavit form under 37 CFR 1.132 to assure correctness and statutory guarantees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publications may be considered but cannot substitute for required testimonial assurances; declarations provide statutory assurances (35 U.S.C. 25; 18 U.S.C. 1001). (Cites: Ex parte Gray.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus between claimed invention and evidence of commercial success required
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant bears the burden of proving a factual and legal 'nexus' connecting commercial success to the claimed invention for the evidence to be probative of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO relies on applicant to provide hard evidence of commercial success and nexus; sales of products not covered by claims are not probative. (Cites: In re Huang; In re GPAC; In re Paulsen; Demaco v. Von Langsdorff.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success abroad is relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success outside the United States is relevant to a nonobviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign commercial success may be considered along with domestic evidence. (Cites: Lindemann Maschinenfabrik v. American Hoist.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success must be due to the claimed features and be commensurate in scope with the claims being supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits claiming product was 'constructed according to the disclosure and claims' without evidence that sold product corresponds to claimed invention do not establish nexus. Evidence of success due to unclaimed features is insufficient. (Cites: In re Tiffin; Joy Technologies v. Manbeck; Ex parte Standish.)

rubrics_metrics.name: When commercial product is not coextensive with claimed invention, show legal relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: If the commercially successful product/process is not coextensive with the claims, applicant must show a legally sufficient relationship between the claimed feature and the commercial product/process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant need not show success at every point in a claimed range but must show typical operation and persuasive affidavits when claims cover combinations not shown in prior art. (Cites: In re Hollingsworth; Demaco.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must be derived from the claimed invention (not marketing or extraneous factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success must be directly attributable to the claimed features and not the result of heavy promotion, brand loyalty, or other business events unrelated to the merits of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusive statements that sales are due to the invention are entitled to little weight; licensing, advertising, market shifts, or other factors must be considered. (Cites: In re Mageli; In re Noznick; Ex parte Remark; Pentec; In re Fielder; EWP Corp.; Hybritech.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must flow from functions/advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Success of devices within the claims must flow from functions or advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification; success attributable to third-party modifications is not probative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must show claimed features produced the commercial success; improvements by others cannot be credited to the applicant. (Cites: In re Vamco Machine & Tool.)

rubrics_metrics.name: In design cases, establishing nexus between design and commercial success is especially difficult
rubrics_metrics.description: In design patent contexts, commercial success must be clearly attributable to the design itself and not to brand recognition or improved performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide evidence linking sales/preference specifically to the design feature; generic success evidence without attribution is insufficient. (Cites: Litton Systems v. Whirlpool.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales figures must be adequately defined to show commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross sales figures alone do not establish commercial success without context such as market share, time period, or expected sales in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide market-share data, time frame, and baseline expectations to make sales figures probative. (Cites: Cable Electric Products v. Genmark; Ex parte Standish.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-felt need and failure of others require objective evidence of a recognized, persistent unsolved problem
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on long-felt need/failure of others, there must be objective evidence that a recognized, persistent problem existed and was not solved by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the problem was first recognized by the applicant, or lack of prior attempts is evident, long-felt need/failure of others is not supported. Provide historical evidence of recognized unmet need and documented failure by others. (Cites: In re Gershon; Orthopedic Equipment Co. v. All Orthopedic Appliances.)
